lengths/task: Translate the French je suis étudiant, and you get I am a student: three words in, four out. No word-for-word rule can do that.
lengths/one: A recurrent neural network, an R N N, makes one output per token it reads, like a language model guessing at every step. Three tokens in, three out: the fourth word has nowhere to go.
lengths/two: The way around it is two RNNs: the first reads the whole input, and only then does the second write the output, for as many steps as it needs.
lengths/teams: In 2014, two teams built this for translation: Kyunghyun Cho and colleagues, who called it an RNN encoder-decoder, and Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le.
lengths/name: Sutskever's paper, Sequence to Sequence Learning, gave the idea its name: seek two seek, short for sequence to sequence.
readwrite/enc: The first RNN, the encoder, reads the French one token per step, passing its memory, h, along.
readwrite/h: After the last token, h is the encoder's final state: capital H numbers, one per hidden unit, that must hold the whole sentence.
readwrite/code: To encode is to put into a code: the sentence becomes a code of capital H numbers. The second RNN, the decoder, turns that code back out as words.
readwrite/start: The decoder starts from h. Nothing is written yet, so its first input is a start token.
readwrite/first: Like a language model, it gives every token in its vocabulary a probability, and writes the most likely one, the argmax: I.
readwrite/feed: Each word it writes becomes its next input. Reading I, it writes am; then the word a; then student.
readwrite/end: It stops when it writes the end token, which is in its vocabulary too. That is what lets the output be any length.
readwrite/count: So count the decoder's steps: four words, plus the end token, makes five.
readwrite/reads: It also reads five tokens: the start token and the four words. The start token is only read, and the end token only written.
readwrite/total: Add the encoder's three steps, and the whole translation takes eight.
train/training: Now training: nudging every weight, a little at a time, downhill on the loss. The model learns from sentence pairs with known translations.
train/targets: Every decoder step has a right answer, the next word of the true translation, and its guess is scored with cross-entropy: five losses for this pair.
train/mistake: Count the steps from zero, and say step one guesses was, instead of am. That step pays its loss. But what should step two read?
train/tf: In training, it reads the true word, am, not its own guess, so one early mistake cannot throw off the rest of the sentence.
train/name: The true translation acts as a teacher, forcing the right word in at every step: so this is called teacher forcing. Ronald Williams and David Zipser named it in 1989.
train/test: At test time, the trained model meets new sentences with no translation given, so the decoder reads its own last guess, right or wrong.
squeeze/squeeze: One weakness is left. All the decoder knows of the input comes through h: the same capital H numbers, for three words or fifty.
squeeze/cho: Later in 2014, Cho and colleagues measured the cost: their translations got rapidly worse as sentences grew longer.
squeeze/bottle: Like the narrow neck of a bottle, that one vector limits what gets through: it is the bottleneck.
